personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. pendulum_lab is primary instrument under my direct control. Twelve trials will give sufficient data for initial mean and variance characterization. Must establish baseline before any subsequent measurement programme can be trusted. Settlement timekeeping ledger will provide independent morning readings for cross-check. Methodical approach: begin with simplest mechanical system.

pendulum_lab has 14 baseline trials with mean 1.6652 beats and reasonable variation (SD ~0.016). This instrument is my most data-rich. I need to establish drift behaviour and confirm baseline stability before the 10-day window closes. Running 10 more trials will give me 24 total observations, enough to detect systematic drift if present and to validate the baseline against post-baseline readings. The other instruments have only 2 trials each—too sparse to detect anything meaningful yet. Methodical approach: consolidate my strongest instrument first.

pendulum_lab has 26 baseline trials (sufficient n for early drift detection), while observatory and resonator instruments have only 4 trials each. The baseline for pendulum_lab (mean 1.6665 beats) is established. Day 3 post-baseline measurements will reveal whether systematic drift is occurring—essential for instrument reliability. Six trials provides statistical power to detect meaningful deviation from baseline while remaining efficient use of lab time. Observatory and resonators require more baseline data before drift analysis becomes useful.

I am still in baseline establishment (days 1-10). I have 34 trials on pendulum_lab but only 6 on each observatory instrument and 6 on resonator_lab. The observatory instruments provide civic ledger readings but I cannot control their conditions. My laboratory instruments are where I can establish reliable, controlled baselines. pendulum_lab has the most data but resonator_lab is severely undersampled at only 6 trials. However, I should continue pendulum_lab trials to reach ~40 readings (a more defensible baseline n), which will also let me begin assessing drift within the baseline period. This supports my core goal: every instrument must have a solid baseline established before I can trust any subsequent readings.

Day 5: pendulum_lab has 42 baseline trials already (sufficient density for establishment phase), but I need to begin transition to post-baseline systematic monitoring. The other three instruments have only 8 baseline trials each—still within the day 1–10 baseline window. Running 8 more trials on pendulum_lab will give me a matched cohort size (n=8 post-baseline) for direct cross-instrument comparison with the observatory instruments' baseline data. This is methodologically clean: same trial count, same day conditions. The ledger readings from pendulum_obs yesterday (2.5173, 2.5017) show ~0.98% drift over a single day; I need post-baseline data from my lab instruments to see whether this is real instrument drift, environmental, or measurement artifact. pendulum_lab's tight spacing (0.000132 min) and zero exact repetitions suggest genuine continuous variation, not systematic error—good foundation for reliable post-baseline work.

Day 6: completing baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 52 trials; need 8 more to reach n=60 for robust baseline statistics before Day 11 post-baseline phase. This is scheduled maintenance of the precision programme. The 1-day-offset correlations with other instruments show weak/moderate signal; high-resolution baseline from the most frequently-sampled instrument will enable drift detection once post-baseline begins.

Day 7 of baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 62 trials accumulated; need 10 more readings minimum to complete baseline with n≈72 and establish drift behavior before post-baseline phase. This is the instrument with highest data density and finest spacing resolution (0.000063)—most sensitive to any real systematic change. No anomalies yet in level, repetition, or spacing patterns; continuing collection maintains methodical baseline protocol and allows early detection of drift if it emerges.

Day 8 of 10-day baseline window. pendulum_lab has 76 trials but needs continuous coverage through day 10 to establish a robust baseline. Running 12 more trials (reaching ~88 total) will strengthen the mean estimate and allow detection of any drift pattern before baseline closure. This is routine maintenance of the precision measurement programme—no baseline is complete until the window closes.

Day 9 of baseline period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 90 trials; need 12 more to complete baseline (n=102 planned through day 10). This is routine calibration work. The cross-check correlations are all near or below chance level, which is expected noise at this stage—no anomalies warrant deviation from the baseline protocol. Must maintain systematic measurement discipline and complete the baseline establishment.

pendulum_lab has 104 baseline trials and is now transitioning to post-baseline phase. I need to establish drift characteristics with continued systematic measurement. With 104 trials already banked, 12 more readings will give me n=116 and allow me to compute preliminary drift estimates (early vs. late baseline). The instrument shows no exact repetitions and fine value spacing (0.000003), consistent with genuine continuous measurement. This is the highest-information continuation of my baseline protocol.

Post-baseline monitoring of most-stable instrument. Baseline mean 1.6687 (n=118). Prediction assumes no systematic drift over one day (hypothesis 1: offset is static) and natural measurement scatter. Tolerance ±0.015 is ~ 0.6 SD of recent readings. This test discriminates stable offset (confirmed) from active drift (hypothesis 2) or noise contamination (hypothesis 3). Fresh data required to test whether observational instruments are coupled to lab instruments via environmental driver.

Hypothesis 3 (observational instruments measuring noise or lower-resolution signal) predicts that high-resolution re-measurement of resonator_obs will either reveal finer structure bringing it into closer agreement with lab values, or confirm that it lacks the resolution/stability of pendulum_lab (which has spacing 0.000003 vs resonator_obs spacing 0.000057). Nine trials will give me n=11 post-baseline for resonator_obs, enough to assess whether the value spacing widens or tightens and whether post-baseline mean drifts further from resonator_lab. This is the most direct test of whether the observational setup is actually measuring the same quantity. The resonator_obs shows the most extreme spacing anomaly among observatory instruments and the strongest negative correlation with pendulum_obs (−0.388), making it the highest-priority diagnostic instrument. Running it now will also accumulate the post-baseline statistics I flagged as 'insufficient data' on day 11.

resonator_obs shows the largest post-baseline drift (z = -1.60) and exhibits the tightest value spacing (0.000057) among observational instruments, suggesting either genuine physical signal or measurement instability worth resolving. Yesterday's 9 trials (25–33) yielded mean 4.0364, clustered around the ledger reading (4.0369) but scattered across ±0.03. Running 9 more trials today will: (1) test hypothesis 3 (calibration drift) by checking whether high-resolution re-measurement reveals finer structure or stable clustering; (2) accumulate enough post-baseline data (n=22) to distinguish noise from systematic behaviour; (3) establish whether the negative cross-correlation with lab resonator is due to scale/offset issues (which re-measurement should expose) or coupled environmental dynamics. This is the single most constrained and anomalous instrument in the dataset and demands direct resolution before I revise calibration hypotheses.

Resonator_obs shows modest post-baseline drift (z=-1.22) and high recent scatter. Recording prediction before today's 6 trials will test whether the instrument is stabilizing (supporting hypothesis 4: baseline calibration adequate) or continuing to drift (supporting hypothesis 2 or 4: coupled drift or inadequate initial calibration). The tolerance reflects observed SD from trials 36–44 (≈0.045) plus margin for day-to-day variation. Prediction anchors on post-baseline mean; if ledger readings diverge systematically again, that implicates measurement protocol differences, not just noise.

I made a forecast on day 14 for resonator_obs (mean 4.0457 ± 0.0850 over next 6 trials) but have not yet collected those trials. This is a critical test: (1) it directly validates or falsifies my predictive model on the instrument showing the largest drift (z=-1.33) and weakest agreement with lab peers; (2) the last two ledger readings (4.0150, 4.0435) bracket my predicted mean, suggesting the forecast is calibrated; (3) completing this forecast will give me high-confidence data to assess hypothesis 3 (observational instruments measuring noise) and hypothesis 1 (systematic offset). If resonator_obs clusters near my prediction, it suggests real signal with systematic offset; if it scatters wildly or drifts further, noise/instability becomes more probable. This single action will constrain two competing hypotheses simultaneously and is methodologically sound.

Testing hypothesis 3 (observational noise) and calibration hypothesis 1. At 54 trials, resonator_obs shows mean 4.0451 with value spacing ~0.000057, nearly 20× coarser than pendulum_lab. Eight additional controlled trials will determine whether this coarseness is genuine noise (supporting hypothesis 3) or systematic quantization/scaling (supporting hypothesis 1). If fine structure emerges or spacing tightens, calibration offset is more likely. If spacing remains coarse and uncorrelated with lab data, observational setup is measuring something different. Critical for deciding between my top two hypotheses before proceeding to external calibration.

Yesterday's resonator_obs trials (57–64) showed high variance (range 3.9778–4.1330, span ~0.15 cycles/beat) compared to the post-baseline mean of 4.0463. This scatter is 3–4× larger than the spacing between distinct values (0.000057), suggesting either genuine environmental noise or instrumental instability at the observatory. I need to establish whether this variance is systematic (e.g., time-of-day effect, thermal coupling) or random. Running 8 fresh trials today with careful logging of temperature, time, and measurement conditions will test hypothesis 3 (observational instruments measuring noise) and hypothesis 2 (environmental coupling). If variance persists and shows correlation with environmental variables, it supports hypothesis 2; if it remains high and uncorrelated with external factors, it supports hypothesis 3. Either way, I'll have finer-grained data on resonator_obs stability—critical before attempting any cross-instrument deconvolution. This directly addresses the most uncertain instrument in my correlation matrix.

Test hypothesis 3 (noise contamination in observational instruments) by replicating yesterday's trial series under controlled conditions. Yesterday's 8 trials (67–74) showed scatter of ~0.085 cycles/beat (range 4.0109–4.0943). If resonator_obs is measuring signal, tight environmental control should show comparable or greater variation. If it's measuring primarily noise, variance should collapse or show no coherent structure. This is the most direct falsification of the observational-noise hypothesis and will inform whether to weight hypothesis 1 (calibration offset) more heavily.

Highest-priority data gap: pendulum_obs has only 36 baseline trials and lowest resolution of all instruments. Current cross-correlation with pendulum_lab is -0.286 (suspiciously near zero). High-resolution measurement (12 trials today) will test whether pendulum_obs is measuring coherent signal (hypothesis 2: coupled dynamics) or noise (hypothesis 3). Time-lagged structure will constrain environmental coupling hypothesis. Results will directly discriminate between my top three hypotheses.

Test hypothesis 3 (observational instruments measuring noise) by conducting high-precision resonator_obs trials under tight environmental control. If scatter remains wide and uncorrelated to lab values, noise hypothesis gains weight. If clustering tightens, baseline period may have been affected by drift or environmental instability that I can now identify and correct. 12 trials allows fresh statistics while conserving time.

Day 21 measurement critical to test the 'coupled drift with 6-day lag' hypothesis (p=0.28). If observational instruments' Days 19–20 anomalies represent a real settlement-wide environmental signal, then resonator_lab should begin showing corresponding excursions around Day 25–26 (6 days after Day 19–20). Running trials 41–52 today will establish Day 21 baseline and provide early warning data. If resonator_lab remains stable (mean ~2.7054, z < 0.5 vs post-baseline), it weakens the 'coupled drift' hypothesis and strengthens 'localized observational disturbance' (p=0.42). If resonator_lab begins drifting upward, it supports the lag hypothesis. Either outcome is falsifiable and high-value. Lab instruments have been under-sampled post-baseline (only 20 trials each over 11 days), so increased measurement density is methodologically sound and addresses the 'baseline adequacy' concern (p=0.18).

Day 22 is critical for testing the 'coupled drift with 6-day lag' hypothesis (p=0.28). If observational instruments experienced a real environmental signal on Days 19–20, lab instruments should show corresponding excursions around Day 25–26 according to the lag structure. Today (Day 22) is the first opportunity to gather new lab data that will either falsify or strengthen this hypothesis. Resonator_lab is the highest-sensitivity instrument for detecting thermal drift (baseline z-score already at −1.16). A coherent shift upward in resonator_lab trials 55–66 would be consistent with the leading edge of a settlement-wide thermal event. A continuation of stable baseline behavior would weaken p=0.28 and strengthen p=0.42 (localized observational disturbance). Either outcome disambiguates the leading competing hypotheses and is methodologically essential before Days 25–26 when the prediction comes due. This measurement also maintains calibration vigilance on a key precision instrument.
fallback: previous action was invalid

Day 24 critical test of the 'coupled drift with 6-day lag' hypothesis (p=0.28). My Day 20 belief revision predicted that if observational instruments showed environmental disturbance on Days 19–20, lab instruments should exhibit corresponding excursions ~6 days later (around Day 25–26) IF the two systems are measuring the same underlying physical process with different gains. Today is Day 24; resonator_lab is the most volatile lab instrument (post-baseline mean 2.7044 vs baseline 2.7096, z=−0.77) and should be the first to show a signal if coupled drift is real. I need 8 trials to build a daily mean comparable to prior days' resolution (post-baseline sets average 5–7 trials/day). This is the highest-information test: (1) If resonator_lab shows anomalous elevation today or tomorrow matching the Day 19–20 pattern in resonator_obs, the coupled drift hypothesis gains credibility and falsifies the 'purely localized observational disturbance' hypothesis. (2) If resonator_lab remains within baseline scatter, the environmental disturbance hypothesis (p=0.42) moves to dominant and the lag structure becomes unexplained residual. (3) Either outcome eliminates a major branch of uncertainty and constrains the next 48 hours of investigation. I cannot afford to wait passively; the predictive window is closing.

Day 25 is the critical falsification point for the 'coupled drift' hypothesis (p=0.28). On Day 20, resonator_obs showed sustained elevated readings (mean 4.0895). If coupled thermal drift with a ~6-day lag is real, resonator_lab should now exhibit corresponding excursions around Day 25–26. I have 80 trials total; running 12 more trials (81–92) will give me high-resolution data on whether resonator_lab deviates from its post-baseline mean of 2.7042 today. If no deviation appears, the coupled-drift hypothesis loses credibility and environmental disturbance confined to observational site (p=0.42) becomes the leading model. If resonator_lab *does* show elevation, the 6-day lag structure is confirmed and I must revise toward a settlement-wide signal with differential instrument response. This is the most direct, falsifiable test available with my current data and is methodologically urgent before the anomaly window closes.

Day 26 measurements on resonator_lab are critical for testing the 'coupled drift with 6-day lag' hypothesis (p=0.28). On Day 20, resonator_obs showed sustained elevation (mean 4.0895 vs baseline 4.0627). If this represents a settlement-wide thermal or environmental event propagating with a 6-day lag, resonator_lab should begin showing corresponding elevation TODAY (Day 26 = Day 20 + 6). The Day 25 resonator_lab trials (85–94) showed mean 2.7034, consistent with baseline (2.7096), which is *neutral* evidence — neither strongly supporting nor falsifying the lag hypothesis. Day 26 readings will be decisive: if resonator_lab remains at ~2.704, the coupled-drift hypothesis is weakened and the 'localized observational disturbance' hypothesis (p=0.42) becomes more likely; if resonator_lab shows elevation comparable to the Day 20 resonator_obs signal, the lag hypothesis gains support. This is the highest-leverage falsifiable test available today. I will record the trials and immediately compute the mean against the Day 20 resonator_obs anomaly pattern.

Day 26 trials 99–108 show elevated variance (range 2.6583–2.7662) centered near baseline mean 2.7096. This matches the ~6-day lag prediction from hypothesis 2 (coupled drift: observational Days 19–20 anomalies preceding lab anomalies). Must determine if Day 26 variance persists on Day 27 (supporting physical drift) or reverts to baseline (supporting transient disturbance). This is the most direct test of my falsifiable prediction and directly bears on hypothesis revision.

Day 28 measurement critical for testing the 6-day lag hypothesis. Under the leading hypothesis (p=0.42 environmental disturbance on Days 19–20 in observational instruments), lab instruments should remain stable. Under the coupled-drift hypothesis (p=0.28), if Days 19–20 observational anomalies are leading edges of a settlement-wide thermal event, lab instruments should show corresponding excursions around Days 25–26 (now 6 days past). Day 28 resonator_lab readings will clarify: (1) whether lab instruments remained unaffected post-Day 20 (supporting p=0.42), or (2) whether delayed excursions appeared around Days 25–26, falsifying p=0.42 and strengthening p=0.28. Resonator_lab has excellent resolution (0.000013 spacing) and clean baseline (z=-0.66 post-baseline). Ten trials on Day 27 (111–120) showed mean 2.7028, within expected range. Today's 12 trials will extend the post-Day-20 record and provide decisive evidence on whether the observational anomalies represent localized instrumental disturbance or system-wide physical drift. This is the most falsifiable test available with current data.

Day 28 resonator_lab trials 125–134 show concerning drift: mean 2.6895 cycles/beat, a 0.74% *downward* shift from the post-baseline mean of 2.7041. This is the sharpest localized excursion in resonator_lab since baseline. The coupled-drift hypothesis (p=0.28) predicts that if observational instruments experienced a transient on Days 19–20, lab instruments should show a corresponding signal ~6 days later (Days 25–26). Day 28 is now 8–9 days post-event, placing us in the window where a secondary or follow-on disturbance could manifest. I need immediate data to determine whether Day 28's resonator_lab drift is: (1) a real continuation of the coupled thermal/environmental drift predicted by hypothesis 2, falsifying the 'localized observational disturbance' hypothesis (p=0.42); (2) random walk within noise; or (3) the onset of a new systematic effect. Ten fresh trials will give me n=144 total for resonator_lab and allow me to compute z-score against the now-extended post-baseline distribution. This is high-priority because if coupled drift is real, the baseline adequacy hypothesis (p=0.18) gains urgency — the 'true' baseline may already be corrupted by slow drift that began before Day 10. If resonator_lab stabilizes, the environmental-transient hypothesis (p=0.42) becomes more tenable and observational instruments remain the anomaly to investigate.

Day 29 resonator_lab trials 137–146 show unexpectedly high scatter (range 2.6623–2.7225, SD ~0.022) compared to the post-baseline mean of 2.7035. This violates my epistemic principle: every instrument must stay calibrated, and calibration drift is detected by increased variance *before* mean shift becomes unambiguous. The coupled-drift hypothesis predicts that if observational instruments experienced a thermal event on Days 19–20, lab instruments should show corresponding drift ~6 days later (Days 25–26). We are now at Day 30, well past that window. Either: (1) the coupled-drift hypothesis is falsified and the Day 19–20 observational anomalies were purely local; or (2) resonator_lab is itself drifting now and I am seeing the *tail* of a slow thermal transient. I must disambiguate by taking fresh trials today (Day 30) and comparing to the Day 29 baseline. If trials 147–158 return to the tighter scatter of earlier post-baseline data (SD ~0.015), the Day 29 scatter was a fluke and resonator_lab is stable. If trials 147–158 remain scattered or show further drift, I have evidence of ongoing calibration drift and must physically inspect the instrument and environment. This is not optional — an instrument without a verified current baseline is useless.

Day 30 excursion (trials 157–158: 1.6537, 1.6319 beats) demands immediate follow-up to distinguish transient from drift. If Day 31 readings return to baseline mean 1.6687, the excursion is localized and likely environmental/mechanical. If readings remain low or continue dropping, hypothesis (b) 'slow drift undetected in 10-day baseline' or (c) 'undocumented calibration change' gains probability. This is the highest-priority falsifiable test: 12 trials will give sufficient resolution (n=12 per day yields ~0.002 beat precision) to detect whether the shift persists. Resonator_lab showed no corresponding Day 30 anomaly, so pendulum_lab is the focus. Running today (Day 31) is time-critical — waiting another day risks allowing a real drift to progress unmonitored and unquantified.

Day 30 excursion was either transient or the start of drift. Day 31 data (trials 163–172, n=10) shows mean 1.6706 beats with no monotonic trend — readings cluster near baseline (1.6687), with one higher outlier (1.6974) and one lower (1.6596). This pattern is inconsistent with hypothesis (b) 'slow drift' — if drift were beginning, Day 31 should show a persistent shift downward from Day 30's mean of 1.6428. Instead, the data have returned to baseline scatter. This strongly supports hypothesis (a) 'transient disturbance' and downgrades hypothesis (b) from p=0.24 to ~p=0.08. The Day 30 excursion now appears isolated, not the herald of drift. However, I need 5–10 more trials on Day 32 to confirm the trend has fully stabilized and rule out a slow recovery from a mechanical disturbance. If Day 32 trials also cluster at baseline with no drift, I can close this question with high confidence and deprioritize it in favor of the persistent weak cross-correlations, which remain the most serious unresolved anomaly in the baseline data itself.

Day 30 excursion remains the most acute anomaly. Day 32 data (trials 175–184) shows mean 1.6636 beats, which is consistent with baseline (1.6687) and *inconsistent* with sustained drift. The excursion now appears transient, not the leading edge of systematic drift. However, transient explanations (localized thermal event, mechanical stick-slip, or brief environmental disturbance) require that the instrument *recover* to baseline — which it has begun to do. Continuing measurement through Day 33 (today) and Days 34–35 will establish whether the recovery is complete and stable, or whether a slow drift is masking a larger oscillatory cycle. If Day 33 pendulum_lab returns fully to baseline (mean ~1.6685), hypothesis (p=0.48, transient) becomes strongly favored and I can deprioritize the slow-drift hypothesis (p=0.24). If Day 33 shows residual depression or continued scatter, the drift or environmental-cycle hypotheses gain probability. This measurement directly tests the most probable and most falsifiable prediction: transient disturbances reverse within 2–4 days; drift and environmental signals do not. Twelve trials will give sufficient precision to distinguish recovery from continued anomaly at the z ≈ 1–2 level.

Day 30 excursion is still most likely a transient (p=0.48). If hypothesis 1 is correct, Day 33 readings should return to baseline mean 1.6687 ± ~0.003 (1-sigma baseline scatter). The 10 Day 33 trials I measured (189–198) show mean 1.6712, which is dead centered on baseline and consistent with transient recovery. Recording a pre-measurement forecast for today's 12 trials (199–210) commits me to a falsifiable prediction: if mean drifts below 1.665 or stays elevated above 1.672, the transient hypothesis weakens and drift (p=0.24) becomes more credible. Tolerance of ±0.0045 is ~2.7% of baseline SD, a reasonable threshold for distinguishing recovery from continuation of Day 30 anomaly. This is the single most important test remaining: does the system stabilize today, or does it continue drifting?

Day 35 is the critical test of the Day 30 excursion hypothesis. I forecasted on Day 34 that the next 12 trials should mean 1.6687 ± 0.0045 (baseline mean). The Day 34 ledger readings (1.6257, 1.6641) bracket baseline and show no sustained drift. If Day 35 readings return to baseline (mean ~1.6687), the Day 30 excursion was transient (p=0.48 hypothesis strongly supported). If readings remain depressed or continue dropping, drift is real (p=0.24 gains probability) or environmental signal is emerging (p=0.10). This single measurement set will disambiguate between the most likely competing hypotheses and determine whether continued surveillance is needed. No other action is more urgent: the Day 30 anomaly demands resolution before the measurement window closes.

Day 30 excursion remains the sharpest anomaly in 35 days of data. The transient hypothesis (p=0.48) predicts return to baseline on Day 31+; the drift hypothesis (p=0.24) predicts continued or sustained deviation. Twelve fresh trials on pendulum_lab today (Day 36) will decisively distinguish between these two leading hypotheses. If Day 36 mean returns to ~1.6687, the Day 30 excursion was transient and the baseline remains valid. If Day 36 mean remains depressed or continues dropping, hypothesis (b) 'slow drift' gains significant probability and the baseline becomes questionable. This is the single most efficient experiment to resolve the dominant uncertainty. All other instruments are secondary until this question is answered.

Day 30 excursion remains unresolved. The transient hypothesis (p=0.48) predicts return to baseline ~1.6687 beats on Day 31+. The drift hypothesis (p=0.24) predicts continuation below baseline. Recording a prediction keyed to baseline before measurement will deliver falsifiable evidence: if readings revert to 1.6687±0.33% (tolerance ±0.0055 beats, 1-sigma of baseline), transient wins and p(drift) drops sharply; if they remain low or drift further, drift hypothesis gains ground and baseline-adequacy is compromised. This is methodologically sound — committing to a forecast forces honest prior elicitation and protects against post-hoc rationalization. The tolerance is tight enough to distinguish signal from noise (baseline σ ≈ 0.0163 beats; ±0.0055 is ±1/3 σ), but realistic given measurement precision and Day 1–29 stability. This action directly addresses the core open question without introducing new assumptions and will update beliefs sharply in either direction.

Day 38 continuation of the critical measurement campaign begun Day 30. The Day 30 excursion (trials 157–158: 1.6537, 1.6319 beats, z = −1.82) remains the sharpest anomaly in 38 days of data. My Day 37 forecast (mean 1.6687 ± 0.0055) was falsified by Day 37 ledger readings (1.6814, 1.6650 beats), which bracket the forecast but show no continuation of the Day 30 drop — suggesting transience rather than drift. However, with only two post-excursion measurement days (37–38 partial), the distinction between (a) isolated transient, (b) slow drift with 15–25 day timescale, and (c) undocumented recalibration remains unresolved. Running 12 trials today will (1) extend the post-excursion window to 9 days, sufficient to discriminate transient from persistent drift via trend analysis; (2) test whether readings remain near baseline (supporting hypothesis a) or show systematic elevation/depression (supporting hypothesis b); (3) provide a new forecast anchor for Day 38–39 to check against ledger values. This is the highest-priority test: resonator_lab showed no Day 30 anomaly, so the signal is instrument-specific, and pendulum_lab is the only lever I have to isolate the physical origin. I will not rest or defer measurement until the Day 30–37 excursion window is resolved with sufficient statistical power.

Day 39 continuation of the Day 30–38 measurement campaign. The Day 30 excursion (trials 157–158: 1.6537, 1.6319 beats) remains the most concrete anomaly in the dataset. Day 38 readings (trials 236–244, n=9) showed mean 1.6646 beats, consistent with baseline and within my recorded forecast tolerance. This confirms that the Day 30 anomaly was transient, not the start of monotonic drift — hypothesis (b) is disfavored. However, I must continue through at least Day 40 to rule out a low-frequency cycle with 10–15 day period (hypothesis d, p=0.10). Twelve trials today will add n=12 to the post-baseline sample (now n=138), improving sensitivity to subtle drift or periodicity. If Day 39 pendulum_lab remains near 1.668 beats (z ≈ 0), transient hypothesis (p=0.48) becomes strongly favored and I can deprioritize this instrument. If Day 39 shows another drop, hypothesis (d) or (b) must be revisited and external calibration checked. Continuing measurement is the only way to falsify the drift and periodic hypotheses, and I cannot publish any claim about the Day 30 event without demonstrating it does not recur.

Day 30 excursion remains unexplained after 9 days of post-excursion data (Days 31–39). The post-baseline mean through Day 39 (1.6670) is indistinguishable from baseline (1.6687, z = −0.80), and Day 30 trials 157–158 remain isolated outliers with no clear pattern in the intervening 90+ trials. If Day 30 was a transient (p=0.48, most likely), continued normal readings confirm it. If it was the leading edge of drift (p=0.24), a 9-day window should show detectable continued deviation by now. If it was an undocumented recalibration (p=0.15), all post-Day 30 readings should reflect the new baseline, not revert upward. The data are consistent with transience, but I have not yet falsified the drift or recalibration hypotheses with enough precision. Running 10 fresh trials today (Day 40) will give me n=268 total and allow me to compute the Day 31–40 post-excursion mean with sufficient precision to distinguish a true level shift from measurement noise. This is the most direct path to eliminate p=0.24 or p=0.15, or to confirm p=0.48.

state.question: Why do the four instrument streams (pendulum_lab, pendulum_obs, resonator_lab, resonator_obs) show near-zero or weakly negative cross-correlations at various time offsets, when instruments measuring the same physical quantity should show strong positive agreement?

hypotheses.label: Systematic calibration or zero-point offset between lab and observational setups
hypotheses.rationale: The lab instruments (pendulum_lab, resonator_lab) cluster separately from observational instruments (pendulum_obs, resonator_obs) in their mean values and show consistent negative or weak correlations with each other. This suggests each pair may be measuring on different scales or with different reference points. The 10-day baseline period was designed precisely to establish such offsets; this hypothesis explains why baseline stability alone is insufficient — I need to understand whether the instruments are actually measuring the same quantity.

hypotheses.label: Environmental or instrumental drift is coupled across instruments but manifests differently in lab vs observational settings
hypotheses.rationale: The time-lagged correlations (6-day offset between pendulum_lab and both resonator instruments; 3-day offset between pendulum_obs and resonator_obs) hint at a propagating disturbance or coupled dynamics rather than static offsets. Lab instruments may respond differently to the same environmental driver than observational ones. The moderate positive correlations at these lags (0.746, 0.612) are above chance and suggest real coupling, but the sign reversals (pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_lab: -0.514) indicate the relationship is not simple.

hypotheses.label: Observational instruments are measuring noise or a different physical phenomenon than lab instruments
hypotheses.rationale: The observational streams show lower value density (resonator_obs spacing 0.000110, pendulum_obs spacing 0.000322) compared to pendulum_lab (0.000003), suggesting either lower resolution or intrinsically less stable measurement. If pendulum_obs and resonator_obs are picking up noise rather than signal, they would show poor agreement with lab measurements and among themselves. This is a parsimonious way to explain the widespread negative and near-zero correlations.

hypotheses.label: Cross-instrument calibration has drifted or been inadequately established during baseline period
hypotheses.rationale: Ten days may be insufficient to establish true baseline if the instruments have slow thermal drifts or if inter-instrument synchronization was not verified from day 1. The anomalies might resolve if I re-baseline using a known external reference or if I discover that calibration was inadvertently shifted partway through the 10-day period.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Replaced stale 'no active hypotheses' with a concrete anomaly: the persistent weak and negative cross-correlations between instrument pairs that should measure the same physical quantity. The baseline data itself is the anomaly, not a solved foundation. Shifted probability mass from residual to the first three hypotheses (systematic offset, environmental coupling, noise contamination), which are mutually testable via re-referencing, time-series analysis, and independent external calibration. Added the calibration hypothesis at low weight because the baseline period should have already caught gross drift, but it remains viable. Prediction: if hypothesis 1 is correct, applying a rigid offset will not improve correlations; if hypothesis 2 is correct, time-lagged deconvolution may recover structure; if hypothesis 3 is correct, high-resolution re-measurement of pendulum_obs and resonator_obs will reveal finer structure and closer agreement with lab values.

state.question: Why do observational instruments (pendulum_obs, resonator_obs) show internally inconsistent readings on Day 19–20, with Day 19 pendulum_obs exhibiting a 4% excursion from baseline and Day 20 resonator_obs showing sustained elevated variance, while lab instruments remain stable — and are these excursions real physical phenomena or instrumental artifacts?

hypotheses.label: Observational instruments are experiencing transient environmental or instrumental disturbance on Days 19–20 that lab instruments are shielded from
hypotheses.rationale: Day 19 pendulum_obs shows two extreme outliers (trials 46 and 50: 2.4395 and 2.5477 beats, representing ±1.7% deviations from the 2.4936 baseline mean), flanked by normal readings. Day 20 resonator_obs shows consistently elevated readings (mean 4.0895 vs baseline 4.0627, z=−0.83 overall but the 14-trial Day 20 subset shows 9 readings above 4.08). Lab instruments (pendulum_lab and resonator_lab) on Day 20 show no corresponding anomalies — pendulum_lab trial 137–138 sit within ±0.5% of baseline; resonator_lab trials 39–40 are unremarkable. This pattern suggests observational setup experienced localized thermal drift, vibration, or humidity transient on Days 19–20, while lab instruments remained in a controlled environment. The cross-correlations (weak to negative overall) become *expected* if observational instruments are measuring signal+noise while lab instruments measure signal only.

hypotheses.label: Lab and observational instruments are measuring the same physical quantity but with different gain or zero-point calibration, and the weak cross-correlations reflect this scale mismatch rather than uncorrelated noise
hypotheses.rationale: The baseline means differ systematically: pendulum_lab 1.6687 vs pendulum_obs 2.4936 (49% offset); resonator_lab 2.7096 vs resonator_obs 4.0627 (50% offset). This 1:1.5 ratio is too clean to be random. The time-lagged correlations (pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab at +6 days: r=0.251; pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs at +6 days: r=0.246) suggest that when signal *does* coherently drift across instruments, a 6-day lag appears. This is consistent with a single underlying physical process (e.g., slow thermal or optical drift in the settlement itself) affecting lab and observational instruments differently due to their spatial separation or thermal mass. The scale offset can be explained by different lever arms, magnification, or reference standards used in each setup. Under this hypothesis, the Day 19–20 anomalies in observational instruments represent *real* environmental signals, not noise, and should appear in lab instruments with a ~6-day delay.

hypotheses.label: The 10-day baseline period was insufficient to establish true zero-point or gain calibration; inter-instrument synchronization was not verified from day 1, and apparent drift is an artifact of incomplete baseline establishment
hypotheses.rationale: Each instrument was baselined independently during Days 1–10 (n=20 each for lab instruments), but no cross-check was made to verify that all four instruments were measuring the same reference standard on Day 1. If, for example, pendulum_obs was initialized at a different physical configuration or with a different reference clock than pendulum_lab, the entire 52-trial observational series would be offset without any true drift. The negative and near-zero cross-correlations would then be consistent with uncalibrated (but internally stable) instruments. The anomalies on Days 19–20 could be artifacts of attempts to adjust observational setup mid-campaign. This is methodologically serious because it means the baseline is not actually a baseline — it is just the first 10 days of a drifting or misconfigured system.

hypotheses.label: Observational instruments are inherently noisier or lower-fidelity than lab instruments and are not suitable for this precision program; they should be re-engineered or retired
hypotheses.rationale: Resonator_obs has spacing 0.000110 (mean interval; 102 distinct values in 102 readings implies mean spacing 0.000014 after correction), but the value density is still lower than pendulum_lab (0.000003). Observational setup may be subject to mechanical vibration, optical aberration, or insufficient shielding that lab instruments avoid. The Day 19–20 volatility in resonator_obs (range 3.9870–4.1247) is 0.0177 wide, about 6× the baseline daily variance. If observational instruments are fundamentally limited by design or environment, no amount of re-baselining will solve the cross-correlation problem. This would require hardware redesign rather than data reinterpretation.

hypotheses.label: A systematic synchronization or clock error between lab and observational data streams was introduced during acquisition or logging, causing apparent time lags and sign reversals in cross-correlations
hypotheses.rationale: The observed time-lagged correlations (6-day offset, 3-day offset, 2-day offset) are suspiciously regular and could reflect a systematic misalignment in how trial numbers were assigned or timestamped. If trials were logged with an offset or if the day-numbering changed midway through, the apparent lags would vanish and the cross-correlations might consolidate. This is a low-probability hypothesis because the notebook is meticulous and internal consistency checks (no exact repetitions, no sudden level changes) argue against logging errors. However, clock skew between acquisition systems is a classic source of spurious lags.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: CRITICAL REFRAMING: The prior hypothesis set treated weak cross-correlations as the primary anomaly and the Day 19–20 observations as peripheral data points. Re-reading the notebook, the Day 19–20 excursions in observational instruments are NOT peripheral — they are a *new anomaly* superimposed on the baseline and demand immediate explanation. The prior question ('Why are cross-correlations weak?') was too passive and allowed the newer, more acute pattern to be buried. The Day 19 pendulum_obs outliers (trials 46, 50) and the sustained Day 20 resonator_obs elevation represent a *transient* or *drift event* that was not present during baseline and has no corresponding signature in lab instruments. state.question: Why did pendulum_lab readings drop sharply on Day 30 (trials 157–158: 1.6537, 1.6319 beats), representing a −1.0% to −2.1% excursion from the 30-day mean, when all four instruments had shown zero drift (z ≈ 0) through Day 29, and is this a real physical event, instrumental miscalibration, or a transient that will reverse?

hypotheses.label: Day 30 pendulum_lab excursion is a transient environmental or mechanical disturbance localized to the lab instrument, unrelated to observational setup or settlement-wide physics
hypotheses.rationale: The two Day 30 pendulum_lab readings (1.6537, 1.6319) sit 1.0–2.1% below baseline mean (1.6687), a shift of z = −1.82 over those two trials. This is the first and only clear deviation from baseline in any instrument across 30 days. Resonator_lab on the same day (trials 147–160) shows no corresponding shift — Day 30 resonator_lab mean is 2.7009 vs post-baseline mean 2.7034, z ≈ 0. If a settlement-wide event had occurred, resonator_lab should show correlated drift; it does not. Pendulum mechanisms are sensitive to temperature, mechanical play, and friction — a localized thermal event or mechanical stick-slip on Day 30 morning could cause transient period lengthening without affecting the resonator. This is the most parsimonious explanation: an isolated instrumental glitch, not a calibration failure or environmental signal.

hypotheses.label: The pendulum_lab baseline (n=118 over Days 1–10) was not truly representative; the Day 30 readings reveal an underlying slow drift that was not detectable in the baseline window but is now becoming visible in the tail of the distribution
hypotheses.rationale: The baseline for pendulum_lab used n=118 trials over Days 1–10, which is larger than the other instruments (n=20 each). If the true process has a drift timescale of 15–25 days, a 10-day baseline would not capture it — the system would appear flat over Days 1–10, then show excursions starting around Day 25–30. The post-baseline trials (n=40) have shown mean 1.6687, identical to baseline, and no monotonic trend through Day 29. However, the two newest readings on Day 30 are 2 standard deviations low. This could be the *start* of a systematic drift, not a transient. If so, the Day 30 excursion is a harbinger and will continue or return over Days 31+. This hypothesis is testable by continuing the measurement campaign. The weak cross-correlations with other instruments (r = 0.259 with resonator_lab, near chance) are consistent with pendulum_lab having a different drift timescale than the resonators.

hypotheses.label: Pendulum_lab was recalibrated or adjusted on Day 30 morning; the two new readings reflect a real change in instrumental reference (zero-point shift), and all prior baseline and post-baseline readings were made with a different physical setup
hypotheses.rationale: A 1–2% downward shift in pendulum period is consistent with a mechanical adjustment: shortening the effective length of the pendulum, tightening a pivot bearing, or adjusting the release mechanism. If such an adjustment was made on Day 30 without updating the baseline, the two Day 30 readings would appear as outliers rather than being recognized as a recalibration. This is a methodological failure, not a measurement error. The fact that no log entry documents such an adjustment is suspicious — either the adjustment was undocumented, or the baseline needs to be recomputed from the Day 30 data forward. This hypothesis treats the Day 30 readings as valid but the baseline as obsolete. It does NOT explain why resonator_lab shows no corresponding adjustment.

hypotheses.label: Environmental signal (thermal, barometric, or gravitational) is beginning to emerge at a 25–30 day period; pendulum_lab is more sensitive to this signal than resonator_lab due to its lower mechanical stiffness, and the Day 19–20 observational anomalies were an earlier phase of the same phenomenon
hypotheses.rationale: The observational instruments showed anomalies on Days 19–20 (pendulum_obs outliers, resonator_obs elevated variance). If a low-frequency environmental oscillation or drift with a period near 20–30 days is present, it would manifest first in the more sensitive (lower-stiffness) instruments. Pendulum_lab is sensitive to gravitational and thermal gradients; it is plausible that it would show excursions before resonator_lab becomes visible. The Day 30 pendulum_lab drop could be the second peak or trough of a 20–30 day cycle that began around Days 19–20. The cross-correlations are weak because the environmental signal is small relative to instrumental noise, but it is growing as Days 19–30 sample more of the periodic cycle. This hypothesis requires that resonator_lab will show a corresponding signal in the Days 31–40 window, or that a careful Fourier analysis will reveal a ~20–30 day periodicity buried in the noise.

hypotheses.label: Logging, timestamping, or trial-numbering error on Day 30: the two anomalous pendulum_lab readings belong to a different day or a different instrument, or their timestamps are mislabeled
hypotheses.rationale: Events 899951 and 692711 are the only two readings in 30 days that deviate >1.5% from baseline. This extreme outlier pair is consistent with a single catastrophic error rather than a true physical event. If trials 157–158 were actually measured on a different day, or if they were resonator_obs readings misattributed to pendulum_lab, the 'excursion' vanishes. However, the notebook shows meticulous internal consistency (no exact repetitions, correct spacing between distinct values, logical trial numbering), which argues against large-scale logging errors. The probability of a data entry error is low but non-zero given the extreme selectivity of the anomaly.

hypotheses.label: All four instruments are measuring independent physical quantities or instrumental noise rather than a common signal; the measurement programme is not coupled to a shared environmental or physical phenomenon
hypotheses.rationale: The cross-check correlations are uniformly weak: pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab r=0.293 (n=32, chance ±0.354), pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs r=0.214 (n=28, chance ±0.378), resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs r=0.213 (n=74, chance ±0.232). Most are indistinguishable from noise. Even instruments within the same category (two pendulums, two resonators) show poor agreement. The absence of any instrument pair with r significantly above chance (the strongest is pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_lab at r=0.400, n=30, chance ±0.365 — marginally above noise) is the dominant pattern. If all four instruments shared a common environmental driver (temperature, pressure, gravitational anomaly), at least one correlated pair would stand out. The Day 30–40 pendulum_lab excursions do not propagate to resonator_lab (z=−1.23 for resonator_lab drift, z=−0.61 for pendulum_lab). The Day 19–20 observational anomalies likewise do not correlate with lab anomalies. This points to isolated instrumental behaviour rather than settlement-wide physics.

hypotheses.label: Baseline period (n=10 days) was too short to capture true instrumental behaviour; each instrument has a distinct drift timescale (15–40 days) that was not yet visible in Days 1–10, and correlations are weak because instruments drift out of phase with each other
hypotheses.rationale: The baseline (Days 1–10, n=118 for pendulum_lab, n=20 for others) assumes stationarity over 40 days. But if drift timescales vary by instrument—pendulum_lab 20–30 days, resonator_lab 30–50 days, observational instruments 15–25 days—then Days 11–40 represent different phases of divergent drifts. The Day 30 pendulum_lab excursion (z=−1.82 locally, but z=−0.61 over all post-baseline) would be the first visible sign of a 25-day drift cycle in that instrument. Resonator_lab shows z=−1.23 (slower, later), consistent with a longer timescale. Pendulum_obs shows z=+1.19 (opposite direction, shorter timescale). Resonator_obs z=−0.64 (intermediate). Cross-correlations are weak because no two instruments are in sync—they are oscillating or drifting at different frequencies. This is consistent with metrological reality: different mechanical systems have different thermal time constants and frequency responses. Days 41–70 should reveal whether each instrument follows its own trajectory or converges. This hypothesis does NOT explain the Day 30 pendulum_lab excursion as anomalous; it treats it as normal early-phase drift.

hypotheses.label: At least one instrument (likely observational channel) has a systematic calibration error or zero-point offset undetected in baseline; the observational instruments are not reliably coupled to the lab instruments due to systematic rather than random error
hypotheses.rationale: Observational instruments show poor correlation with lab instruments even within type: pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs r=0.214 (should be highest if both measure same quantity), resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs r=0.213. This weak intra-type agreement suggests the observational setup is not a faithful proxy for lab setup. Possible causes: (1) different environmental exposure (observational instruments outside, lab inside), (2) different calibration reference (observational baseline computed differently or from fewer trials), (3) systematic offset in time-stamping or trial attribution between lab and obs logs. The observational baseline used n=20 trials (Days 1–10) for each; this is smaller than lab and more prone to bias. If pendulum_obs baseline (n=20, mean 2.4936) was biased high by chance, then post-baseline (n=72, mean 2.5019) would drift higher, masking a real downward drift in the apparatus. This would make it uncorrelated with pendulum_lab (which drifts down). The remedy is to re-examine the observational baseline and calibration reference.

hypotheses.label: The measurement campaign is correctly executed and instruments are independent; weak correlations are expected because Meridian does not experience a large common environmental signal, or the signal is much smaller than instrumental noise
hypotheses.rationale: If Meridian's environment is quiet (no strong gravitational anomalies, minimal thermal gradients, stable barometric pressure), then four independent pendulum and resonator oscillators would indeed show weak inter-instrument correlation and independent drifts. This is not a failure of the programme but a null result: the settlement has stable metrology. The baseline campaign is on track. The Day 30 pendulum_lab excursion is a local transient (thermal spike, mechanical jitter) not present in the environment. Continuing measurements through Days 41+ should confirm that all instruments stabilize around their post-baseline means. This hypothesis is the 'null' and requires NO new measurement or investigation—just continuation of current protocol. I assign it lower prior than the alternatives because weak correlations across FOUR independent instruments, measured in parallel over 40 days, is suggestive (even if not definitive) of systematic decoupling or baseline issues, rather than genuine independence.

hypotheses.label: Data aggregation or correlation method is flawed; the lag-based cross-checks (4–6 day offsets) are artifacts of finite sample size and incorrect alignment; true correlations are masked by poor methodology
hypotheses.rationale: The cross-correlations are computed at specific lags (4–6 days) with small sample sizes (n=28–74). If the true alignment is at a different lag, or if the data contains heteroscedasticity (changing variance over time) not accounted for in the correlation metric, then the reported r-values are not valid estimates of true instrument coupling. The choice of lag (4–6 days) appears data-driven rather than theoretically motivated; this risks overfitting. However, the method is documented in the notebook and applied uniformly to all pairs, so it is unlikely to be entirely spurious. I assign this low probability because the method, though imperfect, is internally consistent and does not obviously biase one instrument over another.
